title: Israeli and Palestinian publics describe peaceful coexistence as blocked by incompatible territorial claims, fear, violence, control, and accumulated distrust
source_unit: Pew Research Center, Many Israelis and Palestinians Say They Cannot Coexist Peacefully – and Explain Why, 15 September 2026
geography: Adults in Israel and in the West Bank and East Jerusalem surveyed during spring 2026 conflict conditions

observations.period: March 30-May 6, 2026; perceived possibility of peaceful coexistence

denominator.unit: adults surveyed: 1,001 in Israel and 1,038 in the West Bank and East Jerusalem

israel_possible.unit: percent in Israel saying Israel and an independent Palestinian state can coexist peacefully

palestinian_possible.unit: percent in the West Bank and East Jerusalem saying peaceful coexistence is possible

israel_not_possible.unit: percent in Israel saying peaceful coexistence is not possible

palestinian_not_possible.unit: percent in the West Bank and East Jerusalem saying peaceful coexistence is not possible

legitimacy_route.value: public legitimacy for a two-state future is weak on both sides during wartime conditions

observations.method: Pew nationally representative face-to-face surveys in Israel and the West Bank and East Jerusalem, conducted in Hebrew and Arabic during the Iran war and after an initial ceasefire.
observations.uncertainty: The field period was shaped by active conflict; Gaza was not surveyed, and the results do not predict future negotiations or represent all Palestinians.
observations.subgroup: Israeli Jews, Arab Israelis, Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, younger and older adults, and supporters or non-supporters of the Israeli governing coalition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Wartime fear and uncertainty can suppress optimism temporarily; a low current belief in coexistence does not prove permanent rejection of every future settlement.

shared_reasons.value: respondents on both sides cite land, violence, fear, distrust, competing identities, and the belief that the other side does not want peace

israeli_frame.value: Israeli respondents commonly frame an independent Palestinian state as a security or existential threat

palestinian_frame.value: Palestinian respondents commonly identify Israeli control and occupation in the West Bank and East Jerusalem as the central obstacle

trust_route.value: shared historical violence produces parallel but asymmetric threat and injustice narratives that make trust a precondition for political agreement

observations.method: Pew open-ended follow-up questions with qualitative coding of respondents’ own explanations.
observations.uncertainty: Coded themes summarize reported explanations and do not establish the relative causal importance of each reason or eliminate within-group disagreement.
observations.subgroup: Israeli Jews, Arab Israelis, Palestinians, conflict-affected families, workers, communities divided by checkpoints or control, and political constituencies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared reasons such as violence and fear can provide a starting point for mutual recognition, even when the political meanings assigned to them differ.

observations.period: Spring 2026; conditions named by people who see coexistence as possible

denominator.unit: Pew open-ended response coding frame among respondents expressing possibility or conditionality

conditions.value: respondents who see coexistence as possible mention rebuilding trust, concessions, political will, diplomacy, clear borders, and independence

interdependence.value: some Palestinians point to economic interdependence, shared work, trade, and security as reasons peace could be beneficial

interpersonal_route.value: some respondents cite friendships, past cooperation, and everyday coexistence as evidence that political peace is imaginable

agency_test.value: peace legitimacy depends not only on elite agreements but also on whether publics can imagine security, dignity, and viable everyday relations

observations.method: Qualitative coding of open-ended responses from respondents who said coexistence was possible or conditional.
observations.uncertainty: These responses are from a minority and cannot establish a shared program, negotiation mandate, or policy feasibility.
observations.subgroup: Israeli and Palestinian respondents expressing conditional optimism, communities with cross-group relationships, workers, families, and local civic actors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Interdependence and interpersonal contact may sustain daily life without resolving sovereignty, security, justice, or political authority.

lowest_possible.value: the share of Israelis saying coexistence is possible has remained at its lowest level in the series in 2026

majority_not_possible.unit: percent of Israelis saying coexistence is not possible in 2026, the first time above half in this polling series

arab_israeli_nonresponse.unit: percent of Arab Israelis who did not give a substantive answer in 2026

open_test.value: track whether public legitimacy, leadership, security conditions, economic interdependence, and everyday contact can move attitudes after conflict changes

observations.method: Pew comparison of repeated Israeli surveys on whether peaceful coexistence with an independent Palestinian state is possible.
observations.uncertainty: Longitudinal comparisons remain sensitive to wartime context, question wording, nonresponse, and changing political conditions.
observations.subgroup: Israeli Jews, Arab Israelis, coalition supporters, opposition or nonaligned respondents, and adults across age and ideological groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Opinion may shift with security, leadership, diplomacy, or economic change; current pessimism should not be treated as a permanent social equilibrium.

related_sources.claim: International IDEA democracy-conflict analysis provides complementary institutional and peace-security context.
Pew companion analysis provides complementary public views on military and humanitarian assistance during the conflict.

boundary: This record adds an Israel-Palestine public-legitimacy route from territorial claims, security, occupation, violence, trust, work, and economic interdependence through perceived viability of coexistence. It uses conflict-period survey and open-ended evidence, not a negotiation forecast, Gaza public opinion, individual trauma histories, causal conflict analysis, or proof that current attitudes are permanent.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Pew Research Center report page was reviewed for survey samples, field dates, coexistence shares, open-ended reasons, group-specific frames, Israeli longitudinal comparison, and conflict-period limitations.
